Formal Principle (of the Reformation)
FOR-muhl PRIN-suh-puhl
n. phrase (Reformation theology)
From Latin principium formale: forma (form, structure, the ordering element) + principium (first principle, ruling norm). In scholastic theology, the formal principle is the highest authority that gives a body of knowledge its structure and legitimacy. The Reformers identified Scripture as this authority for Christian theology—the rule that rules all rules (norma normans non normata).

Definition · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

The formal principle of the Reformation is sola Scriptura—Scripture alone as the highest authority for Christian faith and practice. It answers the question: By what authority do we know and teach Christian doctrine? The answer of the Reformers was unambiguous: by the written Word of God alone, not by church tradition, papal decree, or human reason standing above Scripture. Paul declares that “all Scripture is breathed out by God,” profitable for teaching, reproof, correction, and training in righteousness, so that the man of God may be “complete, equipped for every good work” (2 Tim 3:16). Isaiah sets the test: “To the law and to the testimony! If they do not speak according to this word, it is because there is no light in them” (Isa 8:20). The psalmist declares: “Your word is a lamp to my feet and a light to my path” (Ps 119:105). Christ Himself, in the desert, met every temptation with “It is written”—Scripture as the sufficient and final appeal (Matt 4:4). The formal principle does not stand alone: it is distinguished from (and depends on) the material principle, which is justification by faith. Together they define the Reformation's intellectual and spiritual architecture. The formal principle determines the court of appeal; the material principle is the central truth that court reveals. The 1689 London Baptist Confession (1.1–10) expounds sola Scriptura as the formal principle in its opening chapter on Holy Scripture.

Webster 1828 Definition

The Reformation's ruling authority for all Christian teaching—sola Scriptura—Scripture alone as the norma normans (the rule that rules all rules), the supreme formal standard by which all doctrine is tested.

FORMAL PRINCIPLE, n. phrase. In Reformation and Reformed scholastic theology, the highest structural authority for Christian doctrine—Scripture alone (sola Scriptura), the norma normans non normata (the rule that rules all rules and is itself ruled by none).

Contrasted with material principle: the formal principle determines the court of appeal (Scripture); the material principle is the central content that Scripture reveals (justification by grace alone through faith alone).

The Reformers inherited the scholastic distinction between formal and material causes and applied it to the Reformation itself. Luther's stand at Worms (1521)—“My conscience is captive to the Word of God”—is the formal principle in action.

The formal principle does not mean Scripture interpreted in isolation: it means Scripture interpreted by Scripture (analogia scripturae), with all tradition, councils, and confessions answerable to it rather than authoritative over it.

Post-Reformation Roman Catholicism placed Scripture and Tradition as coequal sources of divine authority (Council of Trent, 1546); Vatican II (Dei Verbum, 1965) refined but did not retract this. The formal principle is precisely what Trent rejected, and what the Reformation will not surrender.

Key Scripture

2 Timothy 3:16 — "All Scripture is breathed out by God, and is profitable for teaching, for reproof, for correction, for training in righteousness —"

Isaiah 8:20 — "To the law and to the testimony! If they do not speak according to this word, it is because there is no light in them."

Psalm 119:105 — "Your word is a lamp to my feet and a light to my path."

Matthew 4:4 — "But He answered and said, "It is written, 'Man shall not live on bread alone, but on every word that proceeds out of the mouth of God.'"."

Modern Corruption

Rome elevated Tradition and the Magisterium as equal co-authorities alongside Scripture. Modern evangelicalism increasingly supplements Scripture with experience, therapeutic culture, and community consensus, producing a practical abandonment of the formal principle without a formal rejection of it.

expand to see more

The Roman Catholic corruption is explicit and structural: the Council of Trent (1546) declared Scripture and Tradition to be two parallel streams of divine revelation, with the Magisterium (the teaching office of the Church under the Pope) as the authoritative interpreter of both. This makes Scripture materially present but formally subordinate—the Bible cannot be read or applied without the Church's adjudication. Vatican II's Dei Verbum softened the language but did not resolve the fundamental conflict. The Reformers saw this clearly: Rome's real formal principle is not Scripture but the Pope. The debate at Leipzig (1519) between Luther and Eck turned precisely on this—Luther appealing to Scripture and church councils; Eck pointing out that the Pope had already ruled. Luther's reply conceded the Pope's authority had indeed ruled—and that the Pope had erred.

The evangelical corruption is subtler: the formal principle is confessed but practically overridden. When a congregation adjusts doctrine to match cultural expectation, when preaching is shaped by therapeutic need rather than biblical text, when “the community's reading” or “the Spirit's leading” is invoked to overturn plain scriptural teaching, the formal principle has been abandoned in practice. The authority of Scripture is confessed on Sunday and bypassed on Monday. The formal principle demands not merely that Scripture be present in the church but that it govern the church—that no teaching, tradition, or experience be granted authority it exceeds.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

From Latin scholastic theology's principium formale—the ruling structural norm; applied by the Reformers to identify Scripture alone as the supreme authority for Christian doctrine.

expand to see more

Latin forma — form, structure, that which gives shape and order; the formal principle gives Christian theology its authoritative shape.

Latin principium — first principle, starting point; the norm from which all else in theology is governed.

Latin norma normans non normata — the rule that rules and is not ruled by any higher norm; Scripture's unique status as self-authenticating supreme authority.

Sola Scriptura — Scripture alone; the Reformation rallying cry that names the formal principle in its simplest form.

Luther's Worms declaration (1521)—“My conscience is captive to the Word of God; I cannot and will not recant”—the formal principle applied under fire.

Usage

"The formal principle is not anti-tradition; it means tradition serves Scripture, not the reverse—confessions, catechisms, and councils are valuable precisely as they faithfully summarize and transmit Scripture."

"A church that adjusts its doctrine based on cultural pressure, therapeutic need, or community consensus has abandoned the formal principle, whatever its confessional statement says."

"The formal and material principles belong together: without the formal principle, there is no court to which the material principle (justification) can appeal; without the material principle, the formal principle produces orthodoxy without gospel."
